We'll start this chapter by revisiting the idea of radioactive spider bites affecting reaction times. This time, though, we'll move beyond one unusually quick kid and consider a whole sample of Spider-People. That will present a problem: how to determine how likely it is that our sample mean reflects a true change in the population mean. We'll solve it using the tools we've picked up over the last few chapters: $z$-scores, probability, sampling distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem. By putting them together, we'll complete our first hypothesis test.

## Spider-Man revisited

Back in Chapter 5 we considered the possibility that a radioactive spider bite might have improved the reaction times of one individual. We supposed that following the bite, our test subject, Peter Parker, had a reaction time of 189 milliseconds on a test for which the general population had a mean of 284 milliseconds and a standard deviation of 50 milliseconds. We calculated his $z$-score to be $z = \frac{189 - 284}{50} = -1.9$. Assuming reaction times form a normally distributed population, we could then used the unit normal table to find the proportion of scores as fast or faster than his, which turned out to be less than three percent. We decided his score seemed a bit unusual, and we wondered whether it might be evidence that the spider bite had changed his reaction time.

In other words, we asked how probable Parker's reaction time was under the assumption that it came from the population of unbitten kids---that the bite did not affect his reaction time. If we saw a score that was entirely unexceptional, we would have no reason to doubt that assumption. But if we saw a score that was very unusual, we would have reason to question it.

That thought process already contained the basic logic of a hypothesis test: if the spider bite had done nothing, what were the chances of seeing a reaction time this fast or faster? But real research doesn't usually rely on examining just one individual. We usually want a *sample*---a bunch of kids who we treated to radioactive spider bites to see if it would alter their reaction times. Obviously in the real world this experiment probably would not make it past the ethics board, but the Spiderverse™️ provides just such a scenario.

![A sample of my son's toy Spider-People, $n = 3$](resources/figures/3-spidermen.gif){#fig-spidermen}

So say we find three kids, all bitten by radioactive spiders, and we measure their reaction times on the same test. Now the *sample mean* is 189 milliseconds. How does that change our analysis? Is it just as surprising as a single score of 189ms? More surprising? Less? Surprising *enough* to count as evidence that the population mean changed?

{{< include quizzes/08-hypothesis-testing-spider-sample-reflection.qmd >}}

### Null Hypothesis Significance Testing

The move from one Spider-Man to a sample of Spider-People changes the calculation, but the general logic is the same. For Peter's individual score, we used the population distribution to ask what reaction times we would commonly see if nothing had changed. For our sample mean, we'll need the *sampling distribution*---the distribution of all possible sample means for that population and sample size. Once we know its characteristics we can ask what proportion of means are as extreme or more than the one we observed.

Let's attach the key terms to that logic. The formal procedure we're about to use is called *Null Hypothesis Significance Testing*, or *NHST*. The spider bite is the *treatment*: the condition or intervention applied to our sample. A change in reaction times associated with the treatment would be a *treatment effect*, though a significance test alone cannot establish what caused the change. We observe only one treated sample, but we care about the hypothetical population it represents---what would happen if everyone received the treatment. The sample mean is our clue to that population mean.

Under NHST, as the name implies, we begin with a skeptical working model: suppose the spider bites did nothing, so the population of bitten kids still has the same mean reaction time as the population of unbitten kids, 284 milliseconds. This is the *null hypothesis*, $H_0$. The *alternative hypothesis*, $H_1$, says that the population mean changed.

Changed how exactly? We could specify a __directional__ hypothesis. We were kind of assuming that the bites would make the kids faster, so we could say specifically that our alternative hypothesis is that the mean reaction time decreased.

$$H_0: \mu_{\text{bitten}} \ge 284 \qquad H_1: \mu_{\text{bitten}} < 284$$

But we don't really know what to expect. Maybe radioactive spiderbites actually impair performance for all we know, so we could use a __non-directional__ hypothesis: the mean changed in either direction.

$$H_0: \mu_{\text{bitten}} = 284 \qquad H_1: \mu_{\text{bitten}} \neq 284$$

If the null is true, our three Spider-People should behave like a random sample from a population with a mean of 284. But we know that sample means vary due to sampling error, even when the population mean hasn't changed; the sample's mean probably won't be exactly 284ms. So if our treated sample has a different mean, we need to judge whether the difference is more than we would commonly expect from sampling error alone. We do that by imagining the sampling distribution we would get if the treatment had no effect, then asking how common or uncommon our observed sample mean would be in that distribution. We can work out what sorts of sample means that population would commonly produce, then see where our observed mean of 189 falls.

That raises another question: how unlikely is unlikely enough? Before analyzing the data, we choose a *decision criterion*, called *alpha* and written $\alpha$. Say we choose $\alpha = .05$. We're deciding that results in the most extreme five percent of the null distribution will count as sufficiently unusual to reject the null. We'll return to why we might choose that criterion, and how directionality affects it.

Every hypothesis test follows four broad steps: state the hypotheses, set the decision criteria, collect and analyze the data, and make a decision. We'll take a first pass through those steps with the Spider-People, then look back at the choices and reasoning within each one. First, let's work out how unusual our sample mean actually is.

{{< interactive-figure zTestInferentialDiagram makeInferentialDiagram options='{"preset":"z-test"}' fallback="Inferential process diagram for a z test." >}}

## The $z$-test {#sec-spider-test}

There are different kinds of tests we can submit our data to, depending on the nature of the data and the information we have (or assumptions we can make) about the untreated population. The one we'll introduce here is called the $z$-test.

The $z$-test is appropriate when we know the population standard deviation, and the sampling distribution of the mean is normal or approximately normal. The test statistic is a $z$-score that tells us how far our sample mean is from the null hypothesis mean, in units of the standard error of the mean.

$$z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}$$ {#eq-z-test}

In the case of our Spider-People, I told you that we know the original population mean and standard deviation. I also told you we will treat the population as normally distributed. So that makes the $z$-test appropriate here. (But note that I just made up the $\sigma = 50$ and I told you I was taking liberties with the shape of the population. In real research, we rarely know the population standard deviation, so the $z$-test is not used very often. But it is a good place to start.)

Now let's apply the full NHST, $z$-test procedure to our Spider-Sample. We have our hypotheses already: $H_0: \mu = 284$ and $H_1: \mu \ne 284$. We said we should state the decision criterion, alpha, in advance. So let's use the conventional $\alpha = .05$. That means that if our sample mean is in the most extreme five percent of the null distribution, we will reject the null hypothesis. And let's make the hypotheses non-directional, allowing for a change in either direction. With a non-directional alternative hypothesis, we will split that five percent between the two tails of the distribution, giving 2.5 percent in each tail. We can find the $z$-score that cuts off 2.5% in one tail of the distribution in the unit normal table.

{{< interactive-figure criticalZTable makeCriticalValueTable options='{"distribution":"normal","layout":"areas","title":"Unit normal table (excerpt)","z":{"from":1.90,"to":2.00,"step":0.01},"zDigits":2,"areas":["left","right","mean-to-z"],"selected":{"z":1.96,"area":"right"},"maxWidth":"32rem"}' fallback="Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 1.80 to 2.00, with the area to the right of z = 1.96, .025, highlighted." >}}

Since the standardized normal distribution described by the table is symmetrical, the critical values for a two-tailed test are $z = \pm 1.96$. If our sample mean is more than 1.96 standard errors above or below the null mean, we will reject the null hypothesis.

Next, we take our data and calculate the test statistic. First, let's quickly run the numbers with Peter Parker's lone score again, so we have that baseline to compare the sample to. We plug his reaction time of 189 milliseconds into the individual-score equation and get $-1.9$.

$$ z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{189 - 284}{50} = -1.9 $$

That value is not within the critical regions of the null distribution; it is less extreme than the cutoff of $\pm 1.96$ that we obtained from the table above. So now we know that Peter's score is a bit unusual, but not quite extreme enough to reject the null hypothesis, according to our stated $\alpha = .05$.

For the sample of three, we locate the sample mean among all the sample means that the population could produce. The equations from Chapter 7 tell us that this sampling distribution has the same mean as the population and a standard error of $\sigma_M = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$. The Central Limit Theorem tells us about its shape: if the population is normal, the sampling distribution is normal at any sample size; otherwise, it becomes approximately normal as the sample size increases. Because our sample contains only three observations, this calculation relies on our simplifying assumption that reaction times are normally distributed; with a large enough sample size, we could still run the $z$-test even if the population were skewed.

Putting the values into the equation gives us a $z$-score of $-3.29$:
$$ z = \frac{M - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{189 - 284}{50 / \sqrt{3}} = -3.29 $$

The numerator is the same difference we calculated for Peter alone. It's the denominator that changes: we divide by the standard error of the mean rather than the standard deviation of individual scores. 

The $z$-score for the sample of $n = 3$ is quite a bit lower than $-1.9$ for the single score, because sample means vary less than individual scores. A sample mean as far from the population mean as this is less common than an individual score that far away.

And now, the $z$-score for the sample is beyond the critical values we stated above, $\pm 1.96$. That puts the sample mean in the lower critical region, so we would reject the null hypothesis at $\alpha = .05$.

We could, if we wanted, look up that precise $z$-score in the unit normal table, to find its precise probability, rather than just comparing with the critical values. For $z = 3.29$, we get a much smaller lower-tail probability: $P(z \le -3.29) = .0005$. Because our hypothesis is non-directional, an equally extreme result in the upper tail also counts, giving a two-tailed probability of approximately $.0010$.

{{< interactive-figure spidermenZTable makeCriticalValueTable options='{"distribution":"normal","layout":"areas","title":"Unit normal table (excerpt)","z":{"from":3.25,"to":3.33,"step":0.01},"zDigits":2,"areas":["left","right","mean-to-z"],"selected":{"z":3.29,"area":"right"},"maxWidth":"32rem"}' fallback="Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 3.25 to 3.33, with the area to the right of z = 3.29, .0005, highlighted." >}}

To show this visually, here's what the sampling distribution looks like and where our sample mean lies in that distribution. I've included axes for both the original units (milliseconds) and the $z$-scores representing the sampling distribution, and shaded the critical regions red. Remember, the $z$-scores are just a change of label. You can see our sample mean pretty far down in the extreme tail of the distribution.

{{< interactive-figure spidermenSamplingDistribution makeStandardizedScoreGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"normal","mean":284,"sd":28.87,"xDomain":[165,403],"xTicks":8,"zTickValues":[-4,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3,4],"rawAxisSideLabel":"(M, ms)","zAxisSideLabel":"(z)","statGuides":false,"maxWidth":"42rem","shade":{"tail":"two","alpha":0.05},"markers":{"at":189,"label":"M = 189","height":0.45,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"},"animate":true,"ariaLabel":"Sampling distribution of mean reaction times for samples of three, centered on 284 milliseconds with standard error 28.87 milliseconds. The raw-score ruler is aligned above a z-score ruler, the two critical regions beyond z equals plus or minus 1.96 are shaded red, and a vertical line marks the sample mean of 189 milliseconds at z equals negative 3.29."}' fallback="Sampling distribution of mean reaction times for samples of three, centered on 284 ms with standard error 28.87 ms; aligned raw-score and z-score axes show the same positions, the two critical regions beyond z = ±1.96 are shaded red, and a vertical line marks the sample mean of 189 ms at z = −3.29." >}}

In other words, if spider bites leave the population mean at 284 milliseconds, getting a sample of three people with an average of 189 milliseconds is very unlikely. The observed sample is difficult to reconcile with our starting assumption that the bites did nothing. That doesn't prove what caused the difference, but it gives us evidence against the null hypothesis.

{{< include quizzes/08-hypothesis-testing-sample-z-score.qmd >}}

## Hypothesis tests, step by step

Having worked through the $z$-test, let's look back at what we did and let's extract the NHST procedure into a step-by-step process. In doing so, we can elaborate a little on the logic and choices behind each step. When we learn other variations of hypothesis tests, using different statistics, we'll follow the same general steps. The details of the calculations will change, but the logic will remain the same.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

Ronald A. Fisher was a British statistician and geneticist, and one of the central figures in the development of modern statistics. Among many other contributions, he helped develop and popularize significance testing and the use of null hypotheses in experimental research. In his 1935 book *The Design of Experiments*, he put the logic rather neatly:

> “Every experiment may be said to exist only in order to give the facts a chance of disproving the null hypothesis.”
>
> ---R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments* [@fisher1935design, p. 16]

“Disproving” is stronger language than we'll usually use. A statistical result cannot establish with logical certainty that the null hypothesis is false. But Fisher's line captures the direction of the argument: we work out what the null hypothesis predicts, then give the data a chance to contradict it. That doesn't mean we begin by believing that the null hypothesis is true. It gives us a precise model to test.

In our example, the null says that the population mean reaction time remains 284 milliseconds after a bite. The alternative says that the mean changes:

$$H_0: \mu_{\text{bitten}} = 284 \qquad H_1: \mu_{\text{bitten}} \neq 284$$

Notice that the two hypotheses don't play symmetrical roles in this test. The null gives us a specific population mean: 284 milliseconds. Along with our other assumptions, that value defines a specific sampling distribution. It therefore gives us something we can test directly: if the population mean really is 284, how often would we get a sample mean this far from it or farther?

The alternative hypothesis is less specific. It says that the mean is *not* 284, but that could mean 283, 250, 400, or any other value. It doesn't supply one alternative mean from which we could construct one alternative sampling distribution. So it is the null hypothesis that we test directly. The alternative tells us what counts as a departure from it---in this case, a difference in either direction.

That point can be overstated. We *could* specify a particular alternative, such as $\mu_{\text{bitten}} = 250$. That would give us another sampling distribution to work with, and we'll need just such a specific alternative when we discuss statistical power in the next chapter. But our alternative here, $\mu_{\text{bitten}} \neq 284$, does not make one precise numerical prediction.

The null doesn't have to say that two populations are identical in every imaginable respect. It makes a claim about the particular parameter we're testing---the population mean, in this case. In other statistical tests, the null might state that two treatment conditions have equal population means, or that there is no association between two variables. In broad terms, the null says that the particular effect or relationship we're testing is absent.

These two propositions are logical complements: the population mean is either equal to 284 or it isn't. But the evidence isn't perfectly symmetrical. A result that would be very unusual under the null gives us reason to reject it, though it doesn't prove any particular alternative or establish what caused the difference. A result that isn't unusual only means that we fail to reject the null; it doesn't prove the null hypothesis true.

Hypotheses don't have to concern a treatment. Say we're interested in whether there is an association between the number of years of education someone has completed and their lifetime earnings. The null would say that there is no association between education and income. The alternative would say that there is.

- General research question: Is there an association between education and income? 🎓🤑
    - $H_0$: There is no association between education and income.
    - $H_1$: There is an association between education and income.

If you really think about it, this should be by far the most important and effortful step of the entire research process. Formulating new, interesting, sensible, plausible, meaningful hypotheses isn't easy. Even to begin to come up with reasonable and potentially insightful hypotheses requires familiarity with the existing research and theoretical perspectives on the phenomena you're interested in, a coherent definition of the construct(s) in question and a good sense of what makes for a good operational definition. We won't say much more about *formulating* hypotheses for this class. We'll focus more on what happens next: the statistical analysis used to test them.

{{< include quizzes/08-hypothesis-testing-stating-hypotheses.qmd >}}

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

For step two, we're asking, "if the null hypothesis is true, what sample statistics are we most likely or unlikely to see?" The answer depends on the data and the appropriate test statistic, but the general aim is to decide in advance what results would be sufficiently unusual to reject the null.

Here, we need to introduce the terminology of $\alpha$ and $p$-values. The Greek symbol, lowercase $\alpha$, is our decision criterion: a cutoff chosen before we analyze the data. The $p$-value is calculated from the observed data. It is the probability, assuming the null model and its other assumptions are correct, of obtaining a test statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the one we observed. What counts as "extreme" depends on whether our alternative hypothesis is one- or two-tailed.

By convention, psychology often uses an alpha level of .05, placing the most extreme five percent of the null distribution in the rejection region. If our sample's $p$-value is less than $\alpha$, we call the result statistically significant and reject the null hypothesis. So when you see $p < .05$ in a published journal article, this is what it means. Neither number is the probability that the null hypothesis is true. When the null is true and the test's assumptions hold, $\alpha$ is the long-run probability that the procedure will reject it by mistake.

Why five percent? There is nothing mathematically special about it. Ronald Fisher called it a convenient boundary in an influential 1925 statistics book, building on an older rule of thumb that results about two standard deviations from expectation were noteworthy [@fisher1925statistical, pp. 47--48]. The convention stuck, though other thresholds can be more appropriate when the consequences of a false alarm differ.

The **critical region** contains the sample statistics that would lead us to reject the null hypothesis. Its boundary is the **critical value**. For an upper-tailed test with $\alpha = .05$, for example, the critical value is the 95th percentile of the null distribution: 95 percent lies below it, and five percent lies above it.

### One-tailed and two-tailed tests

A one-tailed test has one critical region. A two-tailed test has critical regions at both extremes, dividing the chosen $\alpha$ between them. If $\alpha = .05$, a two-tailed test places two and a half percent at each end of the distribution.

In percentile terms, the two critical values are at the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The middle 95 percent of the null hypothesis distribution lies between them, leaving the most extreme five percent outside them.

Whether we use a one- or two-tailed test depends on how we stated our hypotheses in step one. With a one-tailed, directional hypothesis, the researcher specifies in advance that they are looking for either an increase or a decrease. With a two-tailed, non-directional test, we're looking for a difference in either direction. The main point is that we determine up front what kind of results would lead us to reject the null. We don't choose a convenient tail after seeing the data.

Unless we have a defensible reason to predict a direction in advance, the two-tailed test is the usual choice: it allows results in either direction to count as evidence against the null.

## Explore alpha and critical regions

{{< interactive-figure alphaTutorial makeAlphaTutorial fallback="Explore alpha and critical regions. Use the accompanying steps for an explanation." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Two tails" data-action='{"alpha":0.05,"tail":"two","z":-1.8}'}
The curve shows the sampling distribution of $z$ when the null hypothesis is true. With $\alpha = .05$ split between two tails, the critical values are about $-1.96$ and $1.96$. The shaded regions together contain five percent of the area. Our hypothetical sample has $z = -1.8$, so it falls just short of the lower critical region.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A stricter cutoff" data-action='{"alpha":0.01,"tail":"two","z":-1.8}'}
Reduce alpha to $.01$. The critical regions shrink, and their boundaries move farther from zero, to about $\pm 2.58$. We now require a more extreme result to reject the null. Notice what hasn't changed: the observed $z$ and its $p$-value. Changing our decision criterion doesn't change the evidence in the sample.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A lower tail" data-action='{"alpha":0.05,"tail":"left","z":-1.8}'}
Now compare a plan that put all of $\alpha = .05$ in the lower tail. Its critical value is about $-1.64$, so $z = -1.8$ would lead us to reject the null. A lower-tailed test is relevant when the prespecified alternative predicts a decrease, such as faster reaction times. We're comparing possible plans here; we don't choose the direction after seeing the result.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="An upper tail" data-action='{"alpha":0.05,"tail":"right","z":-1.8}'}
An upper-tailed plan puts the same five percent at the other end. Our negative $z$ doesn't support that alternative, and its upper-tailed $p$-value is large. The direction determines which results count as evidence against the null. It changes both the critical region and the calculation of $p$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Try it" data-action='{"controls-open":true,"alpha":0.05,"tail":"two","z":-1.8}'}
Try changing alpha while keeping the observed $z$ fixed. Then move $z$ across a critical boundary. Crossing into the shaded region and getting $p < \alpha$ are two ways of reaching the same decision. When the null is true and the test's assumptions hold, alpha is also the long-run probability of rejecting it by mistake. It isn't the probability that this particular conclusion is wrong.
:::

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Step three is to conduct the research, gather data, and calculate the appropriate sample statistics. For our purposes, recall that the version of the Central Limit Theorem we're using assumes independent observations drawn from the same population distribution. Random sampling is one way to support those assumptions, though in practice social scientists often collect data in less tidy ways.

The exact statistic we calculate depends on the nature of the data. We'll encounter several others later, including the $t$-test, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and correlation and regression. They all rely on the same fundamental hypothesis-testing ideas we're outlining here.

### Step 4: Make a decision

If the test statistic falls in the critical region---equivalently, if $p < \alpha$---we reject the null hypothesis. Otherwise, we *fail to reject* it. Failing to reject the null isn't the same as accepting it or showing that nothing happened. It means this study did not provide sufficient evidence against it. In the Spider-People example, this was the point at which we compared $z = -3.29$ with the critical values and reached the decision reported above.

## Practice: CBT for OCD

We'll end by having you perform your own hypothesis test. We're going back to the cognitive behavioral therapy example from Chapter 5, based on a study using the Dimensional Obsessive-Compulsive Scale to measure symptoms before and after treatment [@abramowitz2010docs].

And we're going to play the same slightly dishonest teaching trick again. For the moment, pretend that untreated people with OCD form a known reference population with a mean of 30.25 and a standard deviation of 14.89. A treated sample of 40 people has a mean of 15.49. First articulate the null and alternative hypotheses, then set your decision criteria, calculate the test statistic, and make your decision.

I should tell you that, like when I first used this example in Chapter 5, I'm misusing the data here again. As before, the numbers are from the real study, but 30.25 and 14.89 were pre-treatment *sample statistics*, not known population parameters. More importantly, the mean of 15.49 came from the *same 40 people* measured after treatment. That makes this a related-samples design, so this $z$-test is not the analysis we would use for the real study. We'll return to the actual design, and the test it calls for, when we introduce the related-samples $t$-test in Chapter 13.

{{< include quizzes/08-hypothesis-testing-learning-check.qmd >}}

## Summary

NHST gives us a disciplined way to ask whether a sample result is difficult to explain under a null model. But a statistically significant result needn't be a large or important effect. And a nonsignificant result needn't mean that there is no effect. To understand those possibilities, we need to look more closely at effect size, inferential errors, and statistical power. That's where we'll go next.
